Digress

dy-GRESS -- from Latin di- ('aside') + gradi ('to step, walk'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To digress to leave the main subject of a discussion briefly before returning to it.

The tour guide would digress into pirate folklore for a few minutes before steering the group back to the actual lighthouse history.

Worked Example

Every Monday meeting, the CEO would digress into stories about his college rowing team before anyone could bring up the actual budget numbers.

Notice that the CEO always comes back to the budget eventually -- that brief, temporary detour away from the real topic, with a return trip built in, is exactly what it means to digress.

How Digress Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

drift

drift: to move away from something gradually and without much purpose

stray

stray: to wander noticeably far from the correct path or subject

Antonyms

focus

focus: to concentrate attention narrowly on one thing

concentrate

concentrate: to direct all of one's effort onto a single task

How Strong Is It? — drift → digress → stray

drift vs. digress

drift vs. digress: Drift is gentler than digress: attention may drift quietly during a long meeting, while to digress is to step away from the main subject outright before circling back to it.

stray vs. digress

stray vs. digress: The conversation strayed so far from the agenda that nobody remembered what the meeting was originally about.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — di-/dis-

prefix — di-/dis-: aside, apart (Latin)

root — -gress-

root — -gress-: to step, walk (Latin (gradi))

Put it together

Put it together: Digress comes from Latin di- ('aside') plus gradi ('to step, walk') -- so to digress is literally to step aside from the path you were walking, which is exactly what happens when a speaker wanders briefly off-topic.

Use the root in a new word: egress

Use the root in a new word: egress: In case of fire, please use the nearest egress instead of the elevator.

Root Check

Word Choice

Digress describes a brief, often self-aware detour that the speaker eventually returns from -- contrast this with the related word ramble, which describes talking on and on without much structure or focus at all, rather than one short, deliberate side trip.
